issues.legal_issue: An officer empowered to investigate offences under a special narcotics law is not a police officer for the confession exclusion merely because the officer has police-like investigative powers, where the officer cannot file a prosecution report and the law instead requires a formal complaint.
material_facts: The case concerned criminal proceedings under a special narcotics law, in which officers of a revenue intelligence department were empowered to investigate offences.
The accused made self-incriminating statements to those officers during the investigation.
The law provided for cognizance on a police report if the police investigated, but on a formal complaint by an authorised officer if another department investigated.
The officers’ role in arrest and seizure ended with forwarding the arrested person and seized articles as prescribed; they were required to report the arrest or seizure to a superior.
The officers lacked the power to file a report or charge-sheet upon completion of the investigation.
issues.conclusion: The revenue intelligence officers were not police officers within the meaning of section 25 of the Evidence Act, and the accused persons’ confessional statements to them were not barred by that section.
issues.legal_principle: Section 25 of the Evidence Act should be understood broadly in light of its protective purpose, but does not extend to every officer given some police-like powers. Under Badku Joti Savant v. State of Mysore, Romesh Chandra Mehta v. State of West Bengal, Illias v. Collector of Customs, Madras, State of U.P. v. Durga Prasad, and Balkishan A. Devidayal v. State of Maharashtra, a central attribute of a police officer for this purpose is the power to submit a report or charge-sheet on completion of an investigation. Sections 52, 52A and 57 of the narcotics law concerned the handling of arrested persons and seized articles and reporting arrests or seizures; section 36A(1)(d) distinguished a police report from a formal complaint by an authorised officer. The officers’ investigative powers under section 53 did not include the power to submit a report under section 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

predicates.special_narcotics_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an alleged offence under a special law regulating narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances.
predicates.statement_made_to_special_law_investigat: The accused made a confessional or self-incriminating statement to an officer investigating the alleged offence under the special law.
predicates.investigator_lacks_power_to_file_prosecu: The investigating officer cannot conclude the investigation by filing a prosecution report or charge-sheet in court.
predicates.special_law_requires_complaint_for_nonpo: The special law provides for court cognizance on a formal complaint by an authorised officer when an officer outside the police investigates.

issues.definition: If a narcotics proceeding involves a statement to a special-law investigator who cannot file a prosecution report and whose investigation instead leads to a formal complaint, the statement is not barred by the police-confession exclusion.
